analysis.one_liner: Lets the government license federally funded COVID-19 drugs to competitors and cap their prices during health emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in four House committees until the Congress ended in January 2023, with all 27 of its supporters being Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any COVID-19 drug developed with federal support to be licensed to other manufacturers on open, nonexclusive terms, with the patent holder paid a reasonable royalty instead of holding a monopoly. Federal contracts would have to include fair-pricing terms, manufacturers would have to disclose how much public money went into each drug, and if the Health and Human Services Secretary found a pandemic drug's price excessive, the government could void the drug's exclusive marketing rights and license other companies to make it. The bill never moved past its first committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need COVID-19 treatments and vaccines, and the taxpayers and insurers who pay for them, would gain access to cheaper versions of federally funded drugs. Generic and competing manufacturers would gain the right to produce those drugs and pay royalties. People with any condition tied to a declared public health emergency would gain the same protection in future emergencies, since the pricing provisions apply to any covered drug during an emergency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, taxpayers, and generic drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Any COVID-19 drug developed with federal money would have to be licensed on open, nonexclusive terms, so multiple manufacturers could make it instead of one patent holder controlling supply and price.

If HHS determined a pandemic drug's price was excessive — considering access, racial and socioeconomic disparities, public subsidies, and development costs — HHS could void the drug's FDA exclusivity and license any company to make it, with the original holder paid a reasonable royalty.

Manufacturers would have to report how much federal funding, tax credits, and subsidies went into each COVID-19 drug, including research, manufacturing, and patent costs, posted publicly in plain language, with fines of $100,000 per day for failing to file.
Federal contracts for pandemic drug development would have to include fair-pricing terms that account for the value of public subsidies and the drug's effect on access and health program budgets.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug developers and their investors would give up monopoly pricing and exclusive marketing rights on federally supported pandemic drugs, collecting capped royalties from competing manufacturers instead of monopoly profits. Companies would also bear the cost of detailed public disclosure of their development spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patent-holding drug developers and their investors

drawbacks.text: The royalty rate would be capped at no more than the average pharmaceutical royalty rate from IRS tax return data, which developers of high-risk drugs could argue undercompensates them relative to the profits that justify investing in emergency treatments in the first place.

The 'excessive price' determination rests on the HHS Secretary's judgment across six broad factors, which companies would likely contest in court and which could be applied or withheld inconsistently across administrations.

Voiding FDA exclusivity and granting open licenses applies not just to drugs developed with federal support (Section 2) but to any drug used in a declared public health emergency (Section 5), so a company that developed a treatment entirely with private money could still lose its exclusive marketing rights if its price were found excessive.
The disclosure rules reach beyond pricing into executive compensation metrics and marketing budgets, adding compliance costs that go beyond the core goal of affordable treatments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: cheaper pandemic treatments and public visibility into how taxpayer money funds drug development, set against weaker financial rewards for developing emergency drugs and broader government power over private patents. The royalty structure preserves some compensation for patent holders, and applying it to drugs developed with federal support targets the clearest case of public money funding private monopolies. The Section 5 provision reaching all emergency drugs regardless of funding source is the most aggressive part and the most likely to draw a legitimate objection on innovation grounds.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and then to two subcommittees, and no committee ever held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on January 28, 2021, joined by 14 original cosponsors including Doggett, DeLauro, DeFazio, Grijalva, Khanna, Raskin, Jayapal, and Pocan.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Science Space and Technology, and Armed Services — splitting its consideration across committees.

In February and March 2021 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet, and no further action was ever taken.
Over its two-year life the bill gathered 26 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and none of the committees reported it out or scheduled a vote.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and holders of COVID-19 drug and vaccine patents are better off: their monopoly pricing and exclusive marketing rights on federally supported pandemic drugs were never touched, and nothing requires them to disclose how much federal money went into their drugs. Patients and taxpayers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and patent holders

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized Democratic cosponsorship.

for.name: 26 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (Chair Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on February 2, 2021 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Jerrold Nadler, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its intellectual property subcommittee on March 22, 2021 and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Industry whose patents and FDA exclusivities the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Opposed compulsory licensing and price controls on pandemic drugs, the policy area this bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 27 supporters was a House Democrat and no Republican cosponsored, but it never reached a floor vote; it stalled in committees chaired by members of the sponsors' own party.

industries.note: The bill would replace their exclusive rights to federally supported COVID-19 drugs with capped royalties paid by competing manufacturers, and could void FDA exclusivity for any overpriced emergency drug. Their gain from the bill's failure is monopoly pricing on pandemic treatments that patients and taxpayers pay for.
Open, nonexclusive licenses would let them make and sell cheaper versions of covered drugs, referencing the original maker's test data and manufacturing know-how, and pay a royalty.
Companies holding COVID-19 drug patents and exclusivities would see the expected returns on those assets capped at royalty rates, lowering the value of patents developed with public funding.
